exercises.prompt:
What does this line print?

```go
fmt.Print("a", "b", 1, 2, "c\n")
```
hints: `Print` adds a space between two operands only when neither of them is a string.
exercises.solution: Only the pair (1, 2) has two non-strings, so only there is a space added: `ab1 2c`. `Println` with the same arguments would print `a b 1 2 c`, because it always separates operands with spaces.

hints: `%v` prints a slice in square brackets.
exercises.solution: `%d` prints 7, `%s` prints seven, `%v` prints the slice as `[7]`, and `%x` prints 26 in lower-case hexadecimal, `1a`. Output: `7-seven|[7]|1a`.

exercises.prompt: A program imports `"os"` but never uses it. What happens when you run `go build`?

options.label: It fails with the error `"os" imported and not used`.
options.feedback: Yes. Unused imports and unused local variables are compile errors in Go.

options.label: It builds, with a warning.
options.feedback: Not yet. Go has no compiler warnings; the designers made these errors so they can't be ignored.

options.label: It builds, and the unused package is silently dropped.
options.feedback: Not yet. The compiler refuses the program until you remove the import (your editor usually does this for you).

options.label: It fails at run time when `main` starts.
options.feedback: Not yet. This is detected while compiling; nothing runs.

hints: Go is strict about unused code.
exercises.solution: The build fails: `"os" imported and not used`. Go treats unused imports and unused local variables as errors because they are usually mistakes. Editors with gopls remove unused imports automatically on save.

exercises.prompt: Package `geo` declares `func Distance(...)`, `func haversine(...)` and `var Earth`. Which of them can another package use as `geo.Name`?

options.label: `Distance` and `Earth`
options.feedback: Yes. Names beginning with an upper-case letter are exported.

options.label: Only `Distance`, because variables can never be exported
options.feedback: Not yet. Variables, constants, types, functions, struct fields and methods are all exported by the same rule.

options.label: All three, because they are in the same module
options.feedback: Not yet. Visibility is per package, decided by the first letter, not per module.

options.label: None, unless they are listed in an export statement
options.feedback: Not yet. Go has no export statement; capitalisation is the whole rule.

hints: Look at the first letter of each name.
exercises.solution: In Go, an identifier is exported if it begins with an upper-case letter. `Distance` and `Earth` are exported; `haversine` is private to package `geo`.

exercises.prompt: Which statements about the `go` command are true? Choose all that apply.

options.label: `go mod init example.com/hello` creates a `go.mod` file.
options.feedback: Yes. It names the module and records the Go version.

options.label: `go run .` interprets the source code line by line.
options.feedback: Not yet. It compiles the package to a temporary executable and runs that.

options.label: `go build` produces a native executable.
options.feedback: Yes. By default one self-contained file, including the Go runtime.

options.label: `gofmt` lets each team choose its own brace style.
options.feedback: Not yet. gofmt has one standard layout and essentially no style options; that is the point.

hints: Go is compiled; gofmt is deliberately not configurable.
exercises.solution: `go mod init` creates `go.mod` (a) and `go build` produces a native executable (c). `go run` compiles too, into a temporary file (b is false), and gofmt enforces a single standard style (d is false).

exercises.prompt: Go 1.0 shipped in 2012 with the Go 1 compatibility promise. In which year did Go gain generics (type parameters), with Go 1.18?
hints: It was a decade after Go 1.0, after many rounds of design.
exercises.solution: Generics arrived in **Go 1.18, in March 2022**, after more than a decade of discussion about how to add them without making the language harder to read or slower to compile.
